warmup.q: A Parquet file holds 400,000 payments in 4 row groups, written in payment order, so in every row group amount_cents runs from about 100 to about 250,000. How many row groups can a reader skip for WHERE amount_cents > 240000?
options: Three, because only about 4% of the rows match
None, because every row group's range reaches above 240,000
All four, because the filter is pushed down into the file
It depends on whether the file uses Snappy or Zstd
warmup.why: A reader skips a row group only when the min and max in the footer prove that no row can match. Here every row group's max is near 250,000, so each one might hold a match and all four get read. The same rows sorted by amount let a reader skip three of the four. The fraction of matching rows doesn't matter, and compression doesn't change the statistics.

sections.h: A Parquet file is row groups of column chunks, with a map at the end
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track stored a table by column, so a query that needs two columns reads two runs of values and skips the rest. The Storage track's lesson on column stores and compression built the same idea inside one database: each column cut into chunks, each chunk encoded and compressed, with a zone map (its min and max) per chunk. Parquet is that design as a file format, so that Spark, DuckDB, Trino and every other engine can read the same files, and so that a reader on S3 can fetch only the byte ranges it needs. Try to write such a file.

Version 1: one long run per column. Write all 400,000 payment ids, then all 400,000 merchant ids, and so on. This breaks on the writing side. The writer can't put down the first merchant id until it has written the last payment id, so it has to hold the whole table in memory first. A Spark task writing a 10 GB file would need 10 GB of heap.

Version 2: cut the rows into slices and store each slice column by column. Take 100,000 rows, write their payment ids, then their merchant ids, then their amounts. Then the next 100,000. The writer now holds one slice at a time. Parquet calls a slice a row group, and one column's values inside a row group a column chunk. A file with 5 columns and 4 row groups has 20 chunks. Each chunk is stored as one or more pages, the smallest piece a reader decompresses.

Version 3: a reader that wants only the amounts must know where each amount chunk starts. So the writer keeps a map: for every chunk, its byte offset, its size, its encoding, and the smallest and largest value in it. It can only know the offsets after it has written the chunks, so it writes the map last, at the end of the file. The Parquet spec gives exactly this reason: metadata comes last "to allow for single pass writing". The map is the footer. After it come 4 bytes holding the footer's length, then the 4 letters PAR1. The file also starts with PAR1.

So a reader opens a Parquet file from the back, in three steps:

  1. Read the last 8 bytes: the footer's length and PAR1.
  2. Read the footer.
  3. Read only the chunks the query needs, each as one byte range.

On S3, where every read is an HTTP request, that is two small requests (readers often fetch a bigger tail and get the footer with the first one), then exactly the bytes the query needs. The figure below is the picture for the whole lesson.

How big should a row group be? Bigger row groups mean longer runs per column, so fewer, larger reads. They also mean more memory in the writer. The Parquet docs recommend 512 MB to 1 GB. parquet-java, the library Spark writes with, cuts a row group at 128 MB by default (its parquet.block.size setting). The demo below asks DuckDB, the single-machine SQL engine from lesson 1, for 100,000 rows per group so a small file still has four.

try.title: Open a Parquet file from the back
steps: From the labs folder, run FooterDemo. It writes 400,000 payments sorted by amount to build/l04/sorted.parquet, reads the last 8 bytes by hand, and asks DuckDB to decode the footer.
Find the 4 bytes that hold the footer's length and work out their value yourself before you read the next line.
Check one offset: does merchant_id in row group 0 start right where payment_id ends?

code.title: FooterDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import java.io.RandomAccessFile import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.ByteOrder /** Reads the end of a Parquet file by hand, then prints the map of the file its footer holds. */ fun main() { PaymentParquet.open().use { c -> val file = PaymentParquet.sorted RandomAccessFile(file, "r").use { f -> val head = ByteArray(4).also { f.readFully(it) } f.seek(f.length() - 8) val tail = ByteArray(8).also { f.readFully(it) } val footerLength = ByteBuffer.wrap(tail, 0, 4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).int println("file: %s, %,d bytes".format(file.name, f.length())) println("first 4 bytes: %s".format(String(head))) println("last 8 bytes: %s (%s)".format(tail.joinToString(" ") { "%02x".format(it) }, String(tail, 4, 4))) println("footer: %,d bytes, starting at byte %,d".format(footerLength, f.length() - 8 - footerLength)) } // DuckDB decodes the footer for us: one row per column chunk val chunks = c.rows( """SELECT row_group_id, row_group_num_rows, path_in_schema, data_page_offset, dictionary_page_offset, total_compressed_size, stats_min, stats_max FROM parquet_metadata('${file.absolutePath}') ORDER BY row_group_id, column_id""") for ((group, rows) in chunks.groupBy { it[0] }) { println("row group %s: %,d rows".format(group, rows[0][1]!!.toLong())) for (r in rows) { val start = minOf(r[3]!!.toLong(), r[4]?.toLong() ?: Long.MAX_VALUE) println(" %-13s at byte %,10d %,8d bytes min %-10s max %s".format(r[2], start, r[5]!!.toLong(), r[6], r[7])) } if (group == "1") { println(" ... row groups 2 and 3 look the same"); break } } } }

file:          sorted.parquet, 3,631,674 bytes
first 4 bytes: PAR1
last 8 bytes:  0b 09 00 00 50 41 52 31  (PAR1)
footer:        2,315 bytes, starting at byte 3,629,351
row group 0: 100,352 rows
  payment_id    at byte          4   486,462 bytes  min 0          max 399997
  merchant_id   at byte    486,466   115,342 bytes  min 0          max 499
  card_country  at byte    601,808    25,556 bytes  min DE         max NL
  status        at byte    627,364    25,592 bytes  min AUTHORIZED max REFUNDED
  amount_cents  at byte    652,956   257,085 bytes  min 100        max 63031
row group 1: 100,352 rows
  payment_id    at byte    910,041   486,527 bytes  min 4          max 399998
  ...
  amount_cents  at byte  1,563,047   256,142 bytes  min 63033      max 125677
  ... row groups 2 and 3 look the same

(Output trimmed in the middle.) The bytes 0b 09 00 00 are little-endian: lowest byte first, so they mean 0x090b, which is 2,315. Each chunk starts where the one before it ended: 4 + 486,462 = 486,466. The footer is 2,315 bytes for 3.6 MB of data. DuckDB rounded 100,000 rows up to 100,352, a multiple of the 2,048-row batches it works in. The amount ranges climb from one row group to the next because this file is sorted by amount.

sections.h: Encodings shrink each column before compression does
sections.html:
The footer tells a reader where status lives. How many bytes does it take there? The encodings are the ones from the Storage track's column-store lesson. What matters here is what Parquet calls them, who picks them and what they save on real data. The demo writes the same 100,352 payments several ways.

Written PLAIN, every value is stored in full: a 4-byte length, then the letters. AUTHORIZED costs 14 bytes, and the chunk of 100,352 statuses takes 1,254,547 bytes, 12.5 bytes a row for a column with four distinct values. With dictionary encoding, the four strings are stored once at the start of the chunk and each row stores a 2-bit code, packed tightly by Parquet's RLE/bit-packing hybrid: 100,352 x 2 bits is 25,088 bytes, and the measured chunk is 25,577 bytes, almost 50 times smaller. Sort the rows by status and the codes come in four long runs, which run-length encoding stores as "this value, this many times": 99 bytes.

Numbers have delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED): the first value, then the differences. Payment ids 0, 1, 2, 3 shrink from 802,839 bytes to 469. Random amounts follow no pattern, and delta encoding only takes them to 238,907 bytes.

Encodings work on the meaning of the values. On top of them comes compression: a general byte compressor such as Snappy or Zstd, run on each page. Spark compresses Parquet with Snappy unless you set spark.sql.parquet.compression.codec. Zstd is slower to write and usually smaller: the random amounts shrink to 476,459 bytes with Snappy and 309,537 with Zstd.

Two things follow. The writer chooses the encodings, and its settings decide what you get: DuckDB used delta encoding only when asked for Parquet's version 2 encodings (PARQUET_VERSION V2). And dictionaries have a limit. A column of idempotency keys, all different, would need a dictionary as large as the column, so the writer falls back to plain encoding when the dictionary grows too big.

try.title: Write one column five ways
steps: Run EncodingsDemo. It writes the same 100,352 payments several times and prints the size of one column chunk each time.
Before you look: how many bytes does a 2-bit code per row need for 100,352 rows?
Compare the status lines. What did sorting change about the values themselves?

code.title: EncodingsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import java.io.File import java.sql.DriverManager /** * One row group of 100,352 payments, written several ways. For each column it prints the encoding * DuckDB chose and the bytes the column chunk takes in the file. */ fun main() { val file = File("build/l04/encodings.parquet").apply { parentFile.mkdirs() } DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:").use { c -> c.createStatement().use { s -> s.execute("""CREATE TABLE p AS SELECT i AS payment_id, ['AUTHORIZED','CAPTURED','DECLINED','REFUNDED'][(hash(i + 2) % 4)::INTEGER + 1] AS status, (hash(i + 3) % 250000 + 100)::BIGINT AS amount_cents FROM range(100352) t(i)""") } fun show(label: String, column: String, order: String, options: String) { c.createStatement().use { it.execute("COPY (SELECT * FROM p ORDER BY $order) TO '${file.absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet, $options)") } val (encoding, bytes) = c.rows("SELECT encodings, total_compressed_size FROM parquet_metadata('${file.absolutePath}') WHERE path_in_schema = '$column'").single() println(" %-36s %-20s %,10d bytes".format(label, encoding, bytes!!.toLong())) } val raw = "COMPRESSION uncompressed" println("status: 4 distinct values") show("strings, no dictionary", "status", "payment_id", "$raw, DICTIONARY_SIZE_LIMIT 1") show("dictionary + 2-bit codes", "status", "payment_id", raw) show("dictionary, rows sorted by status", "status", "status, payment_id", raw) println("payment_id: 0, 1, 2, 3, ...") show("8-byte values", "payment_id", "payment_id", raw) show("deltas (Parquet v2)", "payment_id", "payment_id", "$raw, PARQUET_VERSION V2") println("amount_cents: random") show("8-byte values", "amount_cents", "payment_id", raw) show("deltas (Parquet v2)", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "$raw, PARQUET_VERSION V2") show("8-byte values, then Snappy", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "COMPRESSION snappy") show("8-byte values, then Zstd", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "COMPRESSION zstd") } }

try.expect:
status: 4 distinct values
  strings, no dictionary               PLAIN                 1,254,547 bytes
  dictionary + 2-bit codes             PLAIN_DICTIONARY         25,577 bytes
  dictionary, rows sorted by status    PLAIN_DICTIONARY             99 bytes
payment_id: 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
  8-byte values                        PLAIN                   802,839 bytes
  deltas (Parquet v2)                  DELTA_BINARY_PACKED         469 bytes
amount_cents: random
  8-byte values                        PLAIN                   802,839 bytes
  deltas (Parquet v2)                  DELTA_BINARY_PACKED     238,907 bytes
  8-byte values, then Snappy           PLAIN                   476,459 bytes
  8-byte values, then Zstd             PLAIN                   309,537 bytes

The first three lines are the dictionary story: 1.25 MB, 25 KB, 99 bytes for the same 100,352 values. PLAIN_DICTIONARY is the old name of the dictionary encoding; with PARQUET_VERSION V2 DuckDB writes the newer RLE_DICTIONARY. 802,839 is 100,352 x 8 bytes plus a few bytes of page header. Sorting changed nothing in the data and made the status column about 250 times smaller.

sections.h: Min and max in the footer let a reader skip whole row groups
sections.html:
A fraud analyst wants every payment above 1,500 euros: WHERE amount_cents > 150000. Column pruning already lets the reader skip the columns the query doesn't name. Can it skip rows too, before reading them?

It can, with the footer. Next to each chunk's offset and size, the footer stores the smallest and largest value in that chunk. Look at the sorted file from the first Try it. Row group 0 holds amounts from 100 to 63,031. No row in it can be above 150,000, so the reader skips the whole row group, every column of it, without reading a byte of data. Row group 1 tops out at 125,677: skipped too. Row groups 2 and 3 might hold matches, so the reader fetches them. The stepper below walks through it.

Skipping data by checking a filter against statistics, inside the file reader, is called predicate pushdown. A predicate is a condition such as amount_cents > 150000. Spark pushes it down from the query into the Parquet reader, which compares it with every row group's min and max. These are the zone maps from the Storage track's column-store lesson, kept in the file itself. Oracle keeps them per range of blocks, and PostgreSQL's BRIN index is one.

Min and max describe a range, not the values inside it. A row group whose amounts run from 100 to 250,099 might hold a 240,000-cent payment, so the reader must open it. That's why the order of rows decides everything. The two demo files hold the same 400,000 payments. In the random file, written in payment order, every row group spans almost the full range, 100 to about 250,000. In the sorted file, each row group covers its own quarter of the range. The next Try it runs amount_cents > 240000 on both. On the sorted file, Spark reads one row group of four. On the random file it reads all four, and the filter throws 96% of the rows away afterwards.

So write files sorted by the column you filter on most. Lesson 4's worked example sorted each day's rows by merchant_id for exactly this reason. One sort can only make one column tidy: the sorted file's merchant_id chunks still run from 0 to 499 in every row group.

Pushdown also needs a reader that uses it. Spark's Parquet reader does (spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown is on by default), and so does DuckDB's.

try.title: The same filter on sorted and random rows
steps: Run SkippingDemo. It runs one query against the sorted file and the random file, in Spark and in DuckDB.
Predict first: the sorted file's row groups start at 100, 63,033, 125,677 and 188,241. How many rows will Spark's scan decode for amount_cents > 240000?
Compare the bytes DuckDB read from each file. Which chunks make up the smaller number?

code.title: SkippingDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col /** * The same filter on the same 400,000 payments, stored sorted by amount and in random order. * Spark reports how many rows its scan handed on; DuckDB reports how many bytes it read. */ fun main() { PaymentParquet.open().use { duck -> val spark = demoSpark() println("SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents WHERE amount_cents > 240000") for (file in listOf(PaymentParquet.sorted, PaymentParquet.random)) { val query = spark.read().parquet(file.absolutePath) .where(col("amount_cents").gt(240_000)) .select("merchant_id", "amount_cents") val matching = query.collectAsList().size if (file == PaymentParquet.sorted) println("Spark's PushedFilters: [${pushedFilters(query)}]") val profile = duck.rows("EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents FROM '${file.absolutePath}' WHERE amount_cents > 240000") .joinToString("\n") { it[1] ?: "" } val read = Regex("""Data Read:\s*([\d.]+ [kMG]?B)""").find(profile)?.groupValues?.get(1) println("%-15s Spark scan handed on %,7d rows, %,d match. DuckDB read %s".format(file.name, scanRows(query), matching, read)) } spark.stop() } }

try.expect:
SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents WHERE amount_cents > 240000
Spark's PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount_cents), GreaterThan(amount_cents,240000)]
sorted.parquet  Spark scan handed on  98,944 rows, 16,200 match.  DuckDB read 382.7 kB
random.parquet  Spark scan handed on 400,000 rows, 16,200 match.  DuckDB read 2.3 MB

Both files give the same 16,200 rows. On the sorted file Spark's scan decoded 98,944 rows, exactly row group 3, and DuckDB read 383 kB, most of it the two chunks of that row group (113,895 + 252,426 bytes). On the random file the scan decoded all 400,000 rows and DuckDB read about 2.3 MB, six times more for the same answer. The 2.3 MB moves a little between runs.

refs.title: Parquet files: configuration and filter pushdown (Spark SQL docs)

sections.h: PushedFilters lists what Spark asked for, not what the file skipped
sections.html:
Spark tells you what it pushed. The scan line of explain() for the query above reads:

FileScan parquet [merchant_id#1,amount_cents#4L] ...
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount_cents), GreaterThan(amount_cents,240000)],
  ReadSchema: struct<merchant_id:int,amount_cents:bigint>

ReadSchema is column pruning: the reader will decode two columns. PushedFilters is the filter Spark handed to the reader. Here is the catch: it is a list of what Spark asked for, not of what the file could skip. There are three common ways to get a long PushedFilters list and skip nothing.

First, a function around the column. WHERE date_format(created_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-07' asks about a string that Spark computes from each row. The footer has min and max for created_at, not for that string, so Spark pushes only IsNotNull(created_at) and reads every row group. Write the filter on the raw column: created_at >= '2026-11-07' AND created_at < '2026-11-08'.

Second, data that isn't sorted by the column. merchant_id = 42 is pushed in full, but every row group holds merchants 0 to 499, so the statistics never rule one out.

Third, a column without statistics. This one surprises people. Spark 4.1 still writes timestamps in the old INT96 type by default (spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType), and parquet-java keeps no min or max for INT96 columns. So a time-range filter on a file Spark wrote with default settings shows up in PushedFilters and skips nothing. Set the type to TIMESTAMP_MICROS, the standard type, and the same filter on the same rows skips about five of every six row groups.

The way to know is to measure. Compare the rows the scan produced with the rows in the table: the "number of output rows" of the scan in the SQL tab of the Spark UI (the web page every Spark application serves, lesson 6), or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in DuckDB.

Min and max can't help with one more case: finding one idempotency key among millions of unsorted ones. Parquet has two optional extras for that. A bloom filter per column chunk answers "could this value be here?" (parquet-java leaves them off by default; DuckDB 2.0 wrote them for the demo file's dictionary columns). The page index stores min and max per page near the footer, so a reader can skip pages inside a row group it has to open.

code.title: PushdownDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Column import org.apache.spark.sql.SaveMode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.date_format import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.hash import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.pmod import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.timestamp_seconds import java.io.File /** * Spark writes a week of 200,000 payments sorted by created_at, in small row groups, twice: with * its default timestamp type (INT96) and with TIMESTAMP_MICROS. Then it runs four filters and * prints what it pushed to the Parquet reader and how many rows the scan handed on. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.conf().set("spark.sql.maxMetadataStringLength", "400") // print PushedFilters in full val payments = spark.range(0, 200_000, 1, 4).select( col("id").alias("payment_id"), pmod(hash(col("id")), lit(500)).alias("merchant_id"), pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(2)), lit(250_000)).plus(100).cast("bigint").alias("amount_cents"), // a random second in the week starting 2026-11-01 00:00 UTC timestamp_seconds(lit(1_793_491_200L).plus(pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(3)), lit(7 * 86_400)))).alias("created_at"), ) val files = mutableMapOf<String, String>() for (type in listOf("TIMESTAMP_MICROS", "INT96")) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", type) val dir = File("build/l04/by-time-$type").absolutePath payments.repartition(1).sortWithinPartitions("created_at") .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).option("parquet.block.size", 256 * 1024).parquet(dir) files[type] = dir } val fromNov7 = col("created_at").geq(lit("2026-11-07 00:00:00").cast("timestamp")) val cases = listOf<Triple<String, String, Column>>( Triple("created_at >= '2026-11-07'", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", fromNov7), Triple("date_format(created_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-07'", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", date_format(col("created_at"), "yyyy-MM-dd").equalTo("2026-11-07")), Triple("merchant_id = 42", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", col("merchant_id").equalTo(42)), Triple("created_at >= '2026-11-07'", "INT96", fromNov7), ) for ((label, type, filter) in cases) { val query = spark.read().parquet(files.getValue(type)).where(filter) val matching = query.collectAsList().size println("WHERE $label ($type file)") println(" PushedFilters: [${pushedFilters(query)}]") println(" scan handed on %,d of 200,000 rows; %,d match".format(scanRows(query), matching)) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-07'   (TIMESTAMP_MICROS file)
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(created_at), GreaterThanOrEqual(created_at,2026-11-07 00:00:00.0)]
  scan handed on 31,502 of 200,000 rows; 28,568 match
WHERE date_format(created_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-07'   (TIMESTAMP_MICROS file)
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(created_at)]
  scan handed on 200,000 of 200,000 rows; 28,568 match
WHERE merchant_id = 42   (TIMESTAMP_MICROS file)
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(merchant_id), EqualTo(merchant_id,42)]
  scan handed on 200,000 of 200,000 rows; 414 match
WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-07'   (INT96 file)
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(created_at), GreaterThanOrEqual(created_at,2026-11-07 00:00:00.0)]
  scan handed on 200,000 of 200,000 rows; 28,568 match

Only the first query skipped anything: the last day of the week is about a seventh of the rows, and the scan decoded 31,502, a little more than the 28,568 that match, because the first row group it reads starts before midnight. The second query returns the same rows and reads everything. The third pushes its filter and still reads everything. The fourth is the first query again, on a file Spark wrote with default settings, and the identical PushedFilters line hides a full scan.

analogy: A Parquet file works like a shipping container with its packing list taped inside the back door. The pallets are row groups, each box on a pallet holds one column's values, and the list says where every box sits and the lowest and highest serial number inside it. A customs officer looking for serials above 240,000 reads the list first and opens only the boxes whose range allows it, and only the box types she cares about. If the serials were packed in order, she opens one pallet. If they were packed at random, every box's range covers everything and she opens them all. The analogy breaks at the list: a real packing list names every item, while the footer only knows each box's lowest and highest value, so a box holding serials 100 and 250,000 and nothing in between still gets opened.
world: Your settlement and authorization data probably reaches the lake as Parquet: a Kafka Connect S3 sink, a nightly Spark export, or a Flink job. Two settings in those writers decide whether later queries can skip anything. If a Spark job writes created_at, set spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType=TIMESTAMP_MICROS, or every time-range query from finance or the fraud team reads every row group. And sort each output file by the column most queries filter on: created_at for time ranges, or merchant_id for per-merchant audits (one of them, since one sort makes one column tidy). An auditor's lookup by idempotency key is the case min and max can't serve. Answer that from Oracle or an index table, or turn on Parquet bloom filters for that column, rather than scanning the lake.
mistake: The common mistake is treating PushedFilters in a Spark plan as proof that the reader skipped data. It only lists the filters Spark offered the reader. Whether anything was skipped depends on the file: on unsorted data every row group's min and max cover the whole range, an INT96 timestamp column has no min and max at all, and a filter wrapped in a function such as date_format or cast isn't pushed in a usable form. All three run correctly and return the right rows, so nobody notices the full scan. Check the scan's output rows (Spark UI SQL tab) or bytes read (EXPLAIN ANALYZE in DuckDB) against the table size. Then fix the cause: filter on raw columns, sort the files by the filter column, and write TIMESTAMP_MICROS.

compare.note: Same 400,000 payments, same columns, same writer. Only the order of the rows differs, and with it the statistics. In payment order each row group is a random sample of the whole table, so its min and max are the table's min and max, and statistics can't rule anything out. Sorted, each row group owns a narrow slice of the range. The random file's payment_id column is the mirror image: in payment order its row groups hold ids 0 to 100,351, 100,352 to 200,703 and so on, so a lookup by payment id skips three row groups there.

worked.title: Make the fraud team's time-range query skip data

steps.say: The fraud team's query over yesterday's authorizations reads the whole day's file even though it asks for one hour. Start with the footer: does the filter column have statistics, and do the row groups' ranges overlap?
steps.code: -- 1. look at the footer of one file, in DuckDB SELECT row_group_id, path_in_schema, type, stats_min, stats_max FROM parquet_metadata('auth/dt=2026-11-06/part-00000.parquet') WHERE path_in_schema = 'created_at'; -- type INT96 and empty stats_min / stats_max: nothing to skip with

steps.say: The writing job uses Spark's default timestamp type. Switch it to TIMESTAMP_MICROS, and sort each day's rows by time inside the file so that each row group covers a short slice of the day.
steps.code: // 2. in the nightly Spark job that writes the day spark.conf().set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS") authorizations .repartition(col("dt")) // one task per day, so one file per day .sortWithinPartitions("dt", "created_at") // neighbouring rows, neighbouring times .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite) .partitionBy("dt") .parquet("s3a://lake/authorizations/")

steps.say: Rewrite the filter on the raw column. A function around created_at hides it from the footer, so only IsNotNull would be pushed.
steps.code: -- 3. before: computes a string per row, pushes nothing useful WHERE dt = '2026-11-06' AND date_format(created_at, 'HH') = '14' -- after: a range on the raw column, compared with each row group's min and max WHERE dt = '2026-11-06' AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-06 14:00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-06 15:00:00'

steps.say: Measure, don't trust the plan. With 24 hours spread evenly over the row groups, one hour should touch about one twenty-fourth of the day's rows, plus at most one row group at each edge.
steps.code: // 4. compare the scan's output rows with the day's rows val q = spark.read().parquet("s3a://lake/authorizations/").where(hourFilter) q.collectAsList() // Spark UI, SQL tab, the Scan parquet node: "number of output rows" // before the fix: every row of the day; after: about 1/24 of them

lab.title: Read a Parquet footer and decide what to skip
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The test class writes two files with DuckDB, the sorted and random files from the Try its, into a temporary folder.
Read ParquetFooter.read, which is already written. It uses parquet-java to decode the footer into RowGroup and ColumnChunk objects: rows, offsets, sizes, min and max.
Write footerLength with a RandomAccessFile. The test decodes the bytes you point at with Parquet's own Thrift classes, so a wrong length fails loudly.
Write RowGroupSkipper.mayContain, then rowGroupsToRead. A chunk with no statistics must always be read.
Write bytesToRead. The test compares your sum with DuckDB's own reading of the footer.

Write SortedWriter.write. The test writes 100,000 payments through it and checks that each row group's amounts start where the last one's ended. Then run all eight tests; one of them checks that Spark's scan decodes exactly the rows of the row groups your code kept.
hints: ByteBuffer.wrap(tail, 0, 4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).int decodes the length. Compare String(tail, 4, 4, Charsets.US_ASCII) with PAR1, and check the first 4 bytes of the file too.
Two ranges overlap when each one starts before the other ends: max >= lo && min <= hi.
rowGroupsToRead should throw IllegalArgumentException for a column the file doesn't have. groups[i].columns[column] returns null then.
For SortedWriter: repartition(1), then sortWithinPartitions(column), then .option("parquet.block.size", rowGroupBytes) on the writer.

drill.title: Skip from the footer
drill.prompt: From memory, write the three decisions a Parquet reader makes before it reads any data: find the footer's length from the file's tail, decide whether a column chunk with a given min and max may hold a value in lo..hi, and add up the bytes it will fetch for a set of columns in a set of row groups.

answer.html: fun footerLength(file: File): Int = RandomAccessFile(file, "r").use { f -> f.seek(f.length() - 8) // [length: 4 bytes LE][PAR1] val tail = ByteArray(8).also { f.readFully(it) } require(String(tail, 4, 4, Charsets.US_ASCII) == "PAR1") ByteBuffer.wrap(tail, 0, 4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).int } fun mayContain(min: Long?, max: Long?, lo: Long, hi: Long): Boolean = min == null || max == null || (max >= lo && min <= hi) // no stats: must read fun bytesToRead(groups: List<RowGroup>, keep: List<Int>, columns: Set<String>): Long = groups.filter { it.index in keep } .sumOf { g -> columns.sumOf { g.columns.getValue(it).bytes } }

recap: A Parquet file is row groups (slices of rows), each holding one column chunk per column, then a footer, a 4-byte footer length and PAR1. The footer is written last so the writer needs one pass.
A reader reads the last 8 bytes, then the footer, then only the chunks it needs as byte ranges.
Encodings shrink a column using its values: a dictionary turns 4 statuses into 2-bit codes, sorting turns them into runs, delta encoding stores differences. Snappy or Zstd compress the result.
The footer's min and max per chunk let a reader skip whole row groups (predicate pushdown). That works only when the rows are sorted or clustered by the filter column.
PushedFilters lists what Spark offered the reader. Functions around a column, unsorted data and INT96 timestamps (Spark's default) all skip nothing. Measure the scan's output rows.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Parquet is columnar, so our time-range queries only read the rows they need." Explain what Parquet actually lets a reader skip, and what has to be true for a time filter to skip anything.
explain.answer: Parquet lets a reader skip two things before decoding data. It skips columns, because each row group stores each column as its own chunk and the footer says where every chunk is: that's column pruning, and it always works. It can also skip whole row groups, because the footer stores each chunk's min and max. A time filter skips a row group only when that row group's min and max for the time column prove no row can match. So three things must be true. The column needs statistics, which Spark's default INT96 timestamps don't have; write TIMESTAMP_MICROS. The rows must be sorted or clustered by time, or every row group spans the whole day and nothing gets ruled out. And the filter must be on the raw column, not wrapped in a function like date_format. Inside the row groups it does read, the reader decodes every row and a filter drops the ones that don't match, so it never reads only the matching rows.

deeper.html:
Parquet has two older relatives you'll meet in the Hadoop world. ORC came out of the Hive project with the same idea under different names: a file is a series of stripes (row groups), each with column streams, indexes holding min and max, and a footer at the end. Hive tables were often ORC, and Spark, Trino and DuckDB read it. Avro is the opposite: a row format. Each record is stored whole, one after another, and the schema is written once at the top of the file. That suits writing one event at a time, which is why Avro is common for Kafka messages with a schema registry, and why Iceberg (lesson 11) keeps its manifest files in Avro. For scans over a few columns of many rows, Avro reads every byte, like the CSV in lesson 1.

One more detail of the footer is worth knowing: string statistics. parquet-java can truncate long min and max strings (parquet.statistics.truncate.length, and 64 bytes for the page index by default), rounding the max up so it still bounds the real values. A truncated range is wider than the true one, so it can only cause extra reads, never wrong answers. That rule holds for all of pushdown: statistics may make a reader read too much, never too little. The filter above the scan always checks every row it gets.
